en: Having prostrated at the feet of the Lord of those who restrain themselves, and likewise before other blessed gurus whose power is kindled by contact with the dust of His feet; the illustrious Veṅkaṭanāyaka composes this auspicious *Nyāyapariśuddhi*, a treatise on logic, which is the abode of stability, through the words of Nārāyaṇa, whose pure body is Bādarāyaṇa.
The elaboration of logic (nyāyavistara) is counted among the fields of knowledge (vidyāsthāna) that are consistent with the Dharma;
however, because it has been corrupted by various [teachers], it is here being purified.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 2. 2.
The position regarding the exclusion of the Gautama-sūtra.

Although it might somehow be possible to include the system of Akṣapāda within the category of the True School (satpakṣa), there is no difficulty comparable to that involved in including it within the school of Kaṇabhakṣa;
nor is its author, Gautama, enumerated among those belonging to the class of darkness (tāmaseṣu).
Nor is there any appearance of deceit;
nevertheless, because he has been excluded by the author of the Brahma-sūtras and others, we do not hold him in high regard.
Indeed, his work is not respected on account of its being of divine origin (ārṣa) or similar qualities.
Because it would lead to an over-extension [of the argument]:
for in the past, the wise one himself first proclaimed the Lokāyata doctrine— the cause of the world's ruin— by means of that very same teacher.
Alternatively, the Grandfather himself is the authority in this matter,
since he taught the Cārvāka doctrine to Indra and Virocana;
likewise, Gautama may also be considered so.
Furthermore:
"The Dharma of the Three Vedas was destroyed by the heretics of the followers of Kaṇāda and Śākya;
previously, it was protected by Viṣṇu, who bears the triple staff."
Thus it is stated in the Smṛti:
"O King, descendant of the Kuru lineage, many are the Puruṣas according to those who investigate Sāṃkhya and Yoga; they do not accept a single Puruṣa."

Furthermore, since it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*: "In brief, however, Vyāsa has declared that [the universe] is of the nature of the one Puruṣa," the exclusion of those [other systems] is appropriate;
if you argue that it is not so in this case [of the Vedānta], we say no.
Because the statement is intended as an illustration due to the equality of the underlying principle;
indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever as to whether it is that or such-and-such.
Even if this position possesses an advantage over other positions by way of the "grasping at kāśa and kuśa grass" logic, [it remains superior].
Moreover, that [objection] does not hold in the proximity of the Vedānta;
for indeed, even a mighty elephant cannot obstruct a lion, however weak the latter may be.
“Since Akṣapāda, the most eminent of sages, proclaimed this treatise for the sake of the world’s peace,
I shall compose a commentary upon it, which serves as the cause for dispelling the ignorance of fallacious logicians.”
This statement, spoken out of partiality for Akṣapāda, is not to be relied upon.
And it has been said by the former teachers:
"Whether it be the system of Kaṇāda, that of Akṣapāda, or indeed the system of Kapila—
all these systems are not systems for the definitive realization of the Self."
Thus it is said.

For this very reason, it is stated in the Sūtra: "By this, those systems not accepted by the learned are also explained"—that is, "by this refutation of the Sāṃkhya position which is not accepted by the Vedas, it should be understood that the positions of the other learned ones who are not accepted by the Vedas—namely, those of Kaṇāda, Akṣapāda, the Kṣapaṇakas, and the Bhiṣaks—are likewise refuted.
Furthermore, no rule is observed that every branch of knowledge must be formally codified in a Sūtra.
Nor is there any royal decree that for each single field of knowledge there must be only one author of sūtras or only one seer (ṛṣi),
since we observe that they were composed by others as well.
The word *pramāṇa* has its etymological derivation both in the sense of "the act of valid cognition" (*bhāva*) and in the sense of "the instrument of valid cognition" (*karaṇa*).
Thus, some maintain that valid cognition itself (*pramā*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
while others hold that it is only the instrument of valid cognition.
3. Others say that it is either one of those two.
4. Valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is knowledge that conforms to conventional reality as it actually exists.

5. That which, through ignorance of it, leads to saṃsāra, and through knowledge of which there is its cessation—that is the object of valid cognition (*prameya*), because it is to be thoroughly known by those seeking liberation.
6. That [object of cognition] is of two kinds, by way of the distinction between substance (*dravya*) and non-substance (*adravya*).

7. Alternatively, the object of valid cognition (*prameya*) is that which is the object of a means of knowledge (*pramā*) in a general sense. 8. Substance is the substratum of adventitious properties (*āgantukadharma*).
9. That which is not thus is non-substantial (adravya).
10. Substance (dravya) is twofold: insentient (jaḍa) and sentient (ajaḍa). 11. The insentient is also twofold: primordial nature (prakṛti) and time (kāla).
12. And likewise, that which is non-inert is twofold: the inward (pratyak) and the outward (parāk). 13. The inward is also twofold: the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara).
14. The outward is likewise twofold: knowledge as an attribute (dharmabhūtajñāna) and the eternal manifestation (nityavibhūti).
Alternatively, substance (dravya) is twofold, through the division of self (ātman) and non-self (anātman).
Or it is threefold, in accordance with the scriptural tradition of the experiencer (bhoktṛ), the experienced (bhogya), and the controller (niyantṛ).
Or it is sixfold, through the division of the three qualities (triguṇa), time (kāla), the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), pure being (śuddhasattva), and intellect (mati).
18. That which is not self-luminous is insentient (jaḍa). 19. That which is self-luminous is non-insentient (ajaḍa).
20. Nature (prakṛti) is that which has a mixed state of being as its substratum.

21. Time (*kāla*) is the cause for the conventional usage of [units such as] moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), and so forth. 22. That which appears to itself is "proximate" (*pratyak*). 23. That which appears to another is "remote" (*parāk*).
24. The individual soul (jīva) is consciousness dependent on another. 25. The Lord (īśvara) is independent. 26. Intellect (buddhi) is the manifestation of objects.

27. Being distinct from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), it is the substratum of existence and possesses eternal glory. 28. It is not a [material] substance, as it exists in manifold ways through the diversity of the qualities of *sattva*, sound, and so forth.
29. Or rather, the supreme Brahman is the primary object of knowledge, being one and distinguished from all else by its preeminence.
30. Because others are established solely in their own selves or solely in Brahman.
31. And because that [Brahman] alone is heard in scripture as being the object of supreme knowledge by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*).
32. Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is knowledge that is the cause of unsettled worldly discourse.
33. Error (viparyaya) is cognition that is the cause of incorrect linguistic usage.
34. Memory (smṛti) is cognition produced solely from mental impressions (saṃskāra). 35. Cognition distinct from that is experience (anubhava).
36. The purpose (*prayojana*) is that which is intended as the goal for human activity.
37. An example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a locus for the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
38. A tenet (*siddhānta*) is a matter accepted by those regarded as authoritative.
39. The members (*avayava*) are the subordinate sentences within the statement of a formal argument (*prayoga-vākya*) that serves as a means of valid cognition for the sake of others.
40. *Tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) is the demonstration of an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa-prasañjana*) regarding the pervader (*vyāpaka*), by way of accepting the pervaded (*vyāpya*).
41. *Nirṇaya* (ascertainment) is the determination of reality (*tattva-avadhāraṇa*) preceded by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) supported by *tarka*.
42. A discussion concerning one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) is a *vāda*.
43. A debate (*jalpa*) is a discussion between those seeking victory, characterized by the establishment of both sides.
44. However, when it lacks the establishment of a counter-position, it is a *vitaṇḍā* (cavil).

45. Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are those that are deficient in one or more of the constituent parts of a valid reason. 46. Quibble (*chala*) is a refutation by superimposing upon a word a meaning that was not intended [by the speaker]. 47. Futile rejoinder (*jāti*) is a refutation that is self-pervasive [in its own fallacy].
48. "The inability to provide a reply is a point of defeat" (nigrahasthāna). 49. Why would such statements not be *sūtras*?
Therefore, in this context, a concise statement concerning definitions and so forth is a *sūtra*.
One should be satisfied by understanding that the *Bhāṣya* and other such works are merely statements providing examples (*udāharaṇa*) and so forth for that [rule].

Nor can there be a fixed rule of priority for what precedes, because that [priority] is possible in those cases, because it would follow that the *Vārttika* could never be introduced, and because in grammar and other sciences, the acceptance of alternative formulations is acknowledged.

Nor should it be thought that Jaimini’s complete agreement with what was stated by Gautama or Kāśyapa follows merely from his indifference toward the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) and so forth; for he relies upon those things well-known in the world for other purposes, just as one might rely on the water in a tank constructed by another.
For even the authors of commentaries on the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*) and others have likewise formulated their own systems of epistemology and so forth, each according to their own way.
Therefore, whatever here is consistent with reason is accepted;
indeed, even the mud found in a pond is not accepted by those of untarnished intellect who descend into it for its water.
Therefore, following the maxim of the lion hidden in the forest, we shall follow the Veda as supported by the logic of things as they truly are, and the logic approved by the Veda,
rather than mere logic alone.

As for that which was stated immediately after citing the passage beginning with "of one who has known the relation" (*jñātasaṃbandhasya*) by Śrī Viṣṇucitta: "The meaning is that inference is an experience containing the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*);

however, in the Nyāya system, there is a determination of its specific details"—that too is intended solely to proclaim the status of this [text] as a branch of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) authorized for its systematic exposition.
Even by the predecessors who, while adhering to that school's position, commented upon the *Pramāṇasamuccaya-sūtra* and other works, some sūtras were occasionally refuted.
This logical principle [of ours] is neither a snake-bite for them,
nor is it a prohibition against using a staff.

And therefore, whether in worldly or Vedic matters, whoever is the speaker— be it an ancient authority or one of the present day— is to be accepted as authoritative, in accordance with common worldly experience and the Vedas.
Lack of clarity regarding the intended meaning, confusion, incompleteness, and bombast—these defects have been categorized as virtues by the dull-witted.
O Blessed One, the sages of old, disregarding the systems of Akṣapāda and others, composed the manual of Nyāya entitled *Nyāyatattva*.

Therefore, by those who followed their own preferred views through various means such as arguments and examples, investigations into the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and other topics were composed in many ways.
Consequently, this position of exclusion from the *Bhāṣya* is established as being like the sun in the sky.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 3.
The position of accepting the Gautama-sūtras.
For those who desire to accept [our position], even the system of Akṣapāda will remain as being of one-pointed consistency with what we have said;
we shall establish it exactly so.
Therefore, we too shall not be at fault by imputing an unintended meaning to the great [teachers].

Since even those [objections] regarding deficient, excessive, or contradictory designations, as well as statements concerning non-defining characteristics and defining characteristics, can be resolved through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) or alternative interpretation (*anyaparyāya*), and since their consistency with that [system] is thereby maintained;
likewise, in this work, wherever there is a clear contradiction with Śruti, Smṛti, or the Śārīraka [Sūtras], that shall be refuted by way of summary.
Regarding what was stated in the first chapter of the Sūtra— "The sense organs, namely the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear, are derived from the elements"—

the mention here of the pentad of cognitive organs (*jñānendriya*) is not intended to exclude other organs. This is because the mind (*manas*) is enumerated separately as an object of knowledge, because its definition is provided immediately thereafter as "the non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind," and because its status as an organ is examined according to the principle of a tenet established by prior acceptance (*abhyupagama-siddhānta*).
Therefore, by the same reasoning and evidence already stated, the group of organs of action (*karmendriya*) is to be understood as sharing the same status;

for while speech is explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, "Activity (*pravṛtti*) is the undertaking of speech, intellect, and body," the four [organs] beginning with the hand are indicated by their function as instruments for bodily activity.

In the *Śārīraka*, however, after proposing the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that “because the sevenfold course is specified,” the venerable Bādarāyaṇa established that the hands and so forth are also sense organs (indriyas), stating: “But the hands and others [are included] when [the body] exists;
therefore, it is not thus.
Furthermore, the phrase “from the elements” (*bhūtebhyaḥ*) does not intend to refer to their material cause (*upādāna*).
This is because that [statement] is also tenable when intended to refer to the nourishment (*āpyāyana*) of the elements by those [senses] derived from *ahaṅkāra*.
And so it is said in the *Vedārthasaṃgraha*: “In this way, the nourishment of the sense organs—which are derived from *ahaṅkāra*—by the [gross] elements is stated in the *Mahābhārata*.
This resolution is for the purpose of applying the same principle to the statements of other sages as well.
Indeed, the task of a scholar consists precisely in resolving mutually contradictory scriptural statements by postulating specific differences in their intended meaning (*tātparya*).

Even for those who maintain that the mind (*manas*) is non-eternal, the Śruti passage, "The mind, my dear, is made of food" (*annamayaṃ hi somya manaḥ*), must be interpreted solely as being concerned with its nourishment.
This same principle applies elsewhere as well.

As for the statements, “Suffering is characterized by affliction” and “Liberation is the absolute release from that,” therein the status of liberation as the absolute cessation of suffering is universally accepted;
yet, bliss (*ānanda*) is not explicitly prohibited there by a direct scriptural statement.
Furthermore, we do not perceive any logical mark (*liṅga*) that is non-erroneously established for that intention.
For this very reason, in the view of the *Bhūṣaṇa*, the attainment of a connection with eternal bliss in liberation (*apavarga*) has been proven.
By this, the statement from the fourth chapter, "Therefore, liberation is the cessation of all suffering," is also fully resolved.
Because even there, there is no negation of bliss.

Furthermore, that which appears here in the second chapter as a defense of the "whole" (avayavin)—seeming to contradict the second chapter of the *Śārīraka*—can also be reconciled as having the same purpose.
For instance: "Nor is there perception of only one part [of the object] because of the existence of the whole."

Because it is yet to be proven, there is doubt regarding the composite whole (*avayavin*). There would be no perception of anything at all if the composite whole were not established; furthermore, the phenomena of supporting and pulling are logically possible [only if such a whole exists].
“If it is argued that [the atom] is perceived like an army or a forest, we say no, because atoms are beyond the senses.
These are indeed those sūtras;
they are not contradicted.

Since there is no contradiction in the fact that the term "whole" (avayavin) refers merely to a specific aggregate that has attained a particular state—intended as its non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa)—due to its being the initiator of the whole in cases such as an army or a forest; and since this alone suffices to account for the specificities of perception and conventional usage;

furthermore, even the statement regarding atoms being beyond the senses is not contradictory, because we accept that even those things which are perceptible, like the parts of a lamp-flame, may become supersensible through a particular change of state.
The followers of the Āgamas maintain that the unmanifest (*avyakta*) itself—the substance consisting of the three *guṇas*—becomes manifest due to a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*).

Even for those things that are individually unfit for perception, perceptibility, degrees of intensity, and so forth, are established in the world even in cases where no composite whole (*avayavin*) has begun, such as in masses of snow or heaps of powder, owing to a specific state of aggregation and a particular form.

As for the justification of another means of knowledge called analogy (*upamāna*), it was formulated by certain Nyāya-partisans solely for the purpose of rejecting the inclusion of analogy within inference.

And as for the objection that— having raised the non-existence of the relationship between word and meaning with the statement, “Because filling, burning, and splitting are not perceived, there is an absence of relationship,” and then having refuted it by stating its conventional nature through such passages as, “The refutation is not [valid] because of the fixed determination of word and meaning,” and “Because the cognition of the meaning from the word is due to convention”— that too should be understood as being intended to demonstrate a specific type of relationship distinct from inference and the like, by means of a conventionality that is universally accepted.

For it is impossible to establish that words existing within the Veda— which possess a tradition that is without beginning or end and uninterrupted— could have a conventional meaning that contradicts the declarations of Manu and others.

As for the statement, "And its authority is like the authority of the Mantras and Ayurveda, because of the authority of the reliable person (āpta)," this too is easily understood as intending that the very Veda, which is without beginning or end, is set forth by the most reliable person, namely Īśvara, at the beginning of every Kalpa exactly as it was before.
The description of the impermanence of phonemes (varṇa), however, is not contradicted by the Śruti and other authorities; on the contrary, it is entirely consistent with them.

For in the *Devatādhikaraṇa* of the *Śārīraka*, having indeed accepted the impermanence of phonemes, [the Sūtras state]: "And therefore there is also permanence," and "There is no contradiction even in the recurrence [of creation], because names and forms are the same, as seen from both perception and Smṛti."
The eternity of the Veda has been established.

As for the fact that they have explained the demonstration of the eternity of phonemes (*varṇa-nityatva*) in Jaimini’s section on words (*śabdādhikaraṇa*), that is merely the fault of the commentators themselves, because that section has a different purpose, namely, that it concerns the eternity of the form of the non-conventional signifier (*asāṃketika-vācaka*).
Furthermore, regarding what was stated at the end of the second chapter— that "the individual, the form, and the genus are the meaning of a word"—
even there we do not see any indication for accepting the *jāti* (genus) as it is postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas;
for here no exhaustive enumeration of categories such as substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), and so forth is being made.

This is because [the previous section] was intended to demonstrate the referents of the "word" (*pada*) as established by the rule "those ending in case-suffixes are a word. Immediately thereafter, he states the definition of only three [categories]: "Individuality (*vyakti*) is form (*mūrti*), the substratum of specific qualities"; "Configuration (*ākṛti*) is that which expresses the mark of a genus (*jāti*"); and "Genus (*jāti*) has the nature of producing similar [cognitions]. However, in this context, these should be applied as appropriate, with reference to the nature of the object itself, its specific defining properties, and the properties that define its essential nature.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the Vedānta even in the second chapter.

In the third chapter, such [sūtras] as "Because a single object is apprehended through both seeing and touching," as well as the investigation into external and internal sense organs and so forth, are extremely useful.
Furthermore, the eternality of the mind and other such matters were not formulated as sūtras therein.
By which [reasoning] there would be a contradiction with the scriptural statements concerning its arising and so forth.

And as for what was stated here—"It consists of the five elements because of [the presence of] odor, moisture, heat, structure, and the provision of space, and because of the authority of scripture"—this very point should be accepted as the established tenet exactly as it is heard. Furthermore, regarding the determination of qualities: "Of odor, taste, form, touch, and sound, those ending with touch belong to earth; by excluding each preceding one, the remaining belongs to water, fire, and air, while the latter alone belongs to space. Thus is the arrangement of qualities established.
Even if one accepts that very point there, there is no contradiction with other entities;
for although sound and so forth are enumerated in the Purāṇas in the sequence of one, two, three, four, and five in relation to ether and the rest,
it is possible to explain that sound exists elsewhere than in what has entered into ether, or that touch and the others exist in each subsequent element due to their entry into earth and the rest.
Since the establishment [of the relationship] through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is equal in both cases,

the *Gandhādi-sūtra*— which states that odors and so forth "exist" in earth— is to be understood as excluding non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*), meaning they definitely exist there. However, in the case of the statement "the latter belongs to space," it is to be understood as excluding connection with anything else (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*), meaning that it belongs to space alone.
And how many such sūtras are interpreted by others as being afflicted?

And as for the objection: “If it is asked why the sense organs do not perceive their own qualities,” and the answer given there—“Because the sense organs possess their qualities”—was countered by the statement, “Because sound is perceived [by the ear]. In that case too, since the auditory organ is nourished by space (*ākāśa*), the answer was formulated by attributing the quality of the nourisher to the quality of the organ, just as in the cases of the blue color of cloth or the fragrance of water. Alternatively, this answer was given with a hidden intention, while remaining within the position that the organs are nourished by the elements, for one who does not understand the origin of the organs from *ahaṅkāra* according to the scriptures. Thus, the objection was addressed through a concealed purpose.
This is what is meant: do you assert that there is no perception of the qualities of the sense organs themselves, or rather that there is no perception of the qualities that nourish them?
In the former case, our own admission is the answer.
Because sound and the other [objects] are not qualities of the sense organs,
there is no deviation [of the reason] in the subsequent case;
therefore, there is no contingency of contradiction with the Vedānta.

In the fourth chapter—namely, the definition of activity (*pravṛtti*) such as attachment and aversion; the demonstration of post-mortem existence (*pretyabhāva*) through the eternity of the self (*ātman*) and so forth; and the examination of the arising of entities without a cause, the non-eternality of all things, and the eternality of all things—is entirely consistent [with the Sāṃkhya system].
The consequence of [infinitesimal] parts should be understood according to the reasoning previously stated.
As for the fifth [category], it is exhausted merely as a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) or a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), and it does not contribute to reality in any way.

Furthermore, matters such as the elegance or lack thereof in the investigation of the factors of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) should be disregarded by those who possess expertise in the reflection upon the actual logic of definitions and the characterized, insofar as they follow the mere established state of things.

Furthermore, when those who follow the later [tradition] obstruct the Vedic paths by introducing the doctrines of Kaṇāda and Caraka under the pretext of the *Kuśakāśāvalambana* in their *Akṣapāda-pañcādhyāyī*,
Gautama himself surely laughs within at that.
Thus ends the position of acceptance.
Alternatively, there may be neither excessive exclusion nor excessive acceptance;
here too, as in the Sāṃkhya and other systems, there would be a meditative absorption that is like well-husked rice.
It is included among the branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) because of its great utility;
it is excluded from the *Sūtras* and other such works because its subject matter consists solely of contradictory portions.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 4.
An analysis of the qualified candidates.
And this elaboration of logic has a restricted scope;
indeed, this elaboration of logic is restricted by its specific subject matter.
Out of compassion and his own greatness, the Teacher declared that there shall be no fault [in its application].

This statement that [the opponent] possesses authority over everything is spoken without due consideration; for how can those who have not studied the scriptures understand the contents of the scriptures?
Or how could one who incites others to what is forbidden be compassionate?
Furthermore, it is impossible to refute the inference regarding the purity of a human head and so forth.

Even there, subversion occurs in two ways: by abandoning the scripture and by means of perception and so forth; for [the former] is due to a lack of qualification regarding the Veda, while [the latter] is due to the lack of stability in anything other than that.
How could Śūdras and others be capable of refuting the disturbance of the Dharma?
Furthermore, even if it were said that another person places their trust in what is spoken by those of the three higher castes; [that too would be insufficient].
When perception and inference are eternally independent of the Veda, one's own investigation into logic results in one's own lack of qualification [to understand it].
In that regard, the *Apashudrabhashya* states that even Shudras and others are entitled [to study];
furthermore, the Blessed One [Manu] declared that there are fourteen branches of both Dharma and Vidyā.
"One must not be touched by Śūdras," so he spoke in the *Aśvamedhika* [Parvan].
"The limbs [of the Veda], the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, the expansion of Nyāya,
the Purāṇa, and the Dharmaśāstra— these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge."
O Bhārata, those branches of knowledge which I have correctly described were produced as purifying sciences for the very purpose of purification.
Therefore, those [objects] must never be touched by a Śūdra under any circumstances. Thus [it is said].
Therefore, these [Vedas] must be studied by those belonging to the three higher castes.
Among them, they must be mastered by a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of acquiring knowledge and for the performance of dharma;
by a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, however, solely for the performance of dharma.
Likewise, Śaṅkha, having enumerated the branches of knowledge (vidyāsthāna), stated: "A Brāhmaṇa is authorized in these; he also demonstrates the means of livelihood for the others.
This very point has been supported by the compilers of the Dharmaśāstras.

Consequently, it is established that for those who possess the qualification for investigating the objects of knowledge— namely, reality and the beneficial, which are to be understood through the inquiry into karma and Brahman— it is precisely they who have the qualification for the extensive treatises on Nyāya, which are intended as a branch of learning (vidyāsthāna) concerning dharma, because these treatises culminate in the ultimate purport [of those inquiries].
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 5.
The determination of the purpose.

The purity of both words and their meanings is established through means of valid cognition such as direct perception; there is a fixed determination of the instruments of knowledge and their objects, and the validity of the teaching is due to its being faultless.
In cases such as the statement regarding stones floating, there is a transfer of meaning (*anyaparyaya*) due to contradiction;
in cases such as the *Citrā* sacrifice yielding cattle, there is a subsumption by way of non-sublation (*abādha*).
The consideration of restatement, injunction, and so forth, which presupposes [the establishment of] attainment and the like,
could not be conceived in any way if perception and the other means of knowledge were unestablished.
By means of such applications, the sages proclaimed the expansion of logic (nyāyavistara) as a field of knowledge concerning dharma, because it serves to support the Vedas.
But when the means of valid cognition known as scripture has been thoroughly purified through the Nyāya-vistara,
the investigation of its specific details shall establish the authoritative status of Dharma.
The complete purification of the object of knowledge also ultimately arises from the contemplation of Brahman;
however, its placement here is for the sake of establishing its purpose and so forth.
The primary subject matter of this treatise is indeed *pramāṇa* (the means of valid cognition).

In this regard, for the sake of establishing the desire to act among discerning persons, it is intended here merely as a demonstration to make known the purpose through a traditional sequence: that the knowledge of the reality of the objects of cognition (*prameya*) is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by way of rejection and acquisition, and that this [knowledge] in turn arises from *pramāṇa* along with its ancillaries.

Therefore, because it has the primary object as its domain and because it establishes the objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is mentioned before the object of cognition.
In that context, the fourteen [categories] beginning with doubt are also examined, as appropriate, by way of their being excluded or their being constituent parts and so on.

Nor is there any insistence on the number sixteen, because it is possible to provide a classification or enumeration that is either fewer or more than that— depending on other limiting conditions such as "not being so" (atathātva) or "error" (viparyaya)— and because there is no difference in terms of utility or lack thereof.
This, indeed, is the very intention of Gautama as well.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 2, Section 6.
The establishment of the distinction between valid and invalid means of cognition.
There exists, indeed, this well-established public highway of worldly and investigative discourse, according to which "this is a means of valid cognition" and "this is not a means of valid cognition.
If that were disregarded, however, investigation itself would not even arise, as it would lack any basis.

For the worldly transaction of the world occurs with reference to some objective basis; it is not that such a basis does not exist in general, but rather its specific nature is what is being investigated.
When the general object has been ascertained but a specific detail is desired to be known,
investigation is indeed appropriate, consisting in the production of a valid cognition regarding one's own intended object.
Not everything is non-authoritative, because one's own position is undermined by itself;
nor is everything authoritative, because one's own position is undermined by something else.
The established order of the world is proven for one's own position regardless of whether it is proven or not;
however, your position is not proven in any way whatsoever, whether that [order] is proven or not.

The sublation of one means of valid cognition by another means of valid cognition is refuted by self-contradiction; if that [sublation] were instead effected by what is not a means of valid cognition, then why would there be no proof for that very point?
If it is argued that the establishment of valid cognition does not occur either through invalid cognition or through valid cognition, that is not so;
for its establishment by means of valid cognition protects both oneself and others.
The determination of what is sublated and what is not sublated must also proceed from a means of valid cognition that is itself established;
otherwise, because there would be no establishment due to a lack of stability, there could be no determination at all.
If there were no determination regarding anything at all, neither doubt nor determination could arise;
just as that [determination] is established for one alternative, it is likewise applicable to others.
When the subject and its common features have been previously ascertained, a doubt arises in the form of "Is this it, or is it not? or "Is this it, or is it something else?"
First of all, doubt is not observed in everyone regarding everything;
rather, you, being clever, hold the conviction that "everything is doubtful."
And for one who maintains a doubtful doctrine of non-duality, doubt is never truly resolved;
even after traveling far, your certainty regarding doubt remains impossible to ward off.
Since the distinction between honor and dishonor has thus been established in general terms,
they now proclaim the specific definition in order to eliminate occasional doubts.

In this regard, we have already stated that, due to differences in etymological derivation and intended meaning, some authorities call both the valid cognition (*pramiti*) and its instrument (*tatkaraṇa*) "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) according to their preference, since the authority of the substratum (*āśrayaprāmāṇya*) is not something to be specifically taught.

The phrase "on account of the authority of a reliable person" (*āptaprāmāṇyāt*) means: on account of the validity [of the scripture] which has as its reason the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*).
Indeed, the authority of the speaker does not contribute to the authority of the sentence in worldly speech;
rather, it is the absence of defects in its causes [that does so]. In either case, it is valid cognition alone that must be scrutinized.
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Section 7.
An Examination of the Definition of Valid Cognition.

In this regard, some among our own [school] who accept the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) and do not accept the validity of memory define valid cognition as "correct experience" (*samyaganubhava*);
those who accept both [memory and misapprehension] define it as "knowledge that accords with reality" (*yathārthajñāna*).
Not desiring either of these two [definitions],
they hold that "valid cognition is experience" (anubhūtiḥ pramā);
such are the definitions stated by other proponents.
We, however, say: valid cognition (*pramā*) is knowledge that conforms to conventional reality as it actually exists.

Whether one accepts the theory of the manifestation of the object as it is (*yathārthakhyāti*), non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), or even the manifestation otherwise (*anyathākhyāti*), this [definition] should not be questioned by those who wish to follow worldly practice.
It will be explained that it is not logical for mere memory to have the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa),
because in the world, only uncontradicted memory is accepted as being a valid means of knowledge.
And when one abandons the Buddha's scriptures, the fact that they are rooted in memory is no reason [for their rejection].
Even though pure mindfulness is the root, [defilements] such as pride may still occur incidentally.
Distinguishing error from valid cognition, they do not say that memory is a form of direct perception;
for in your own system, it is clear that the very nature of memory constitutes its lack of authority.
Furthermore, this [explanation] is not tenable in cases such as the illusion of a yellow conch-shell,
for in that instance, the cognition of both the conch-shell and its yellowness arises through the eye alone.
Therefore, whether in regard to effective action (*pratipatti*) or the arising of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*),
the distinction between valid cognition and error is established by their respective correspondence or non-correspondence with reality.
In this very way, the exclusion of error and the like is established;
for whatever constitutes "otherwise-ness" is intended as "contrariety."

Even in theories such as *ātmakhyāti* (self-apprehension) and others, the fact that [the object] is otherwise than it appears cannot be denied; for otherwise, the occurrence of error and its subsequent sublation would be impossible.
This being the case, by parsimony, it remains that either a cognition of one thing as another or its causal complex is the cause of a non-corresponding linguistic convention.
For all [theories], misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) is the lighter option because it is difficult to abandon;
even by its proponent, it cannot be avoided. Therefore, non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is even lighter than that.
To demonstrate that naturalness resides in anyathākhyāti (the theory of misapprehension) and simplicity in akhyāti (the theory of non-apprehension),
both of these were not abandoned in the Bhāṣya;
for Nāthamuni, Miśra, and others have established the proof of yathārthakhyāti (the theory that all cognition is true).
Some have declared this to be a manifestation of power (vaibhava), because it does not conform to the common understanding of the world.
Even if both [the gross form and the subtle form] exist due to pride, one of the two must certainly be present,
either because the other is not perceived as capable of producing an effect, or because it is perceived as capable of producing an effect.
However, the defects of other philosophical systems become manifest of their own accord upon the study of their respective tenets; therefore, something is said here by way of summary.

In that regard, concerning the theory of self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti): Is the cognition that "there is another consciousness" itself directed toward something else, or is it not? If the former, then there would likewise be a cognition of that [other] object; and if so, there would result only a single cognition regarding everything else.
For that cognition which establishes the consciousness of another continuum or a subsequent moment within its own continuum,
indeed penetrates the external [object] by its own nature.

The rule of simultaneous apprehension and the characteristic of the object belong to consciousness itself; thus, even when there is cognition, just as with the object, the identity of knowledge and the object would not exist.
Just as it is accepted that an error occurs despite the falsity of the entire complex of causes such as the defects [of the senses],
so too, even when the substratum is false, the delusion remains unavoidable.
Consequently, only the position of the Mādhyamika remains there;
yet even in that case, there is no deliverance, because it is altogether untenable.
Do you speak of non-existence as worldly or even as supramundane?
A negation that is without a substratum does not apply to the former; nor is the latter a locus for the intellect.

And is reality, which is free from the four alternatives, authoritative or not? In the former case, its existence would be limited to that [cognition]; if it were not so, then the cognition of it would be a non-cognition.
And regarding the appearance of other things as being without a substratum: in this case, does that which is non-existent appear to you as "being here," or not?
In the first case, a substratum is established; in the second case, there is a denial of the very phenomenon of appearance.
Furthermore, by those afflicted with cataracts, the darkness emitted from their own eyes appears as if it were a cluster of hair; in this same way, such [objects] appear.
Even if an object that does not exist were to appear as if it were present,
nevertheless, it would have a substratum, for it is delimited by its own location and so forth.

Others maintain that there is a superimposition of "that" upon an object perceived as "this"; in that case, your [view] involves a superimposition of "thisness" upon it. Thus, the two positions are equal in their practical result.
Regarding the theory of the manifestation of the indeterminable (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*): Is the object defined by you as being indeterminable, or not?
In the first case, there is a manifold contradiction; in the second, our own position is established.
If even the exclusion of both existence and non-existence is perceived as contradictory,
why indeed is the nature of being both existent and non-existent not perceived when it is actually experienced?
If the transcendence of Brahman over that which is void— like something that is neither hot nor cold—
is to be established through such means as its manifestation and sublation, then that [transcendence] is already established for us in this case.
Nor does the sublation of the entire world arise spontaneously;
however, through an unstable reasoning, even Brahman might be touched by sublation.
If it is maintained that the state of being other than existent occurs at the time of destruction, then there would be a contradiction regarding its own time;
furthermore, destruction itself could not be established.
Furthermore, for certain things that are heard to be eternal, there is indeed no perishability;
therefore, the reason [put forward] is partially unestablished (bhāgāsiddha), and there is no identity between destruction and sublation.

Regarding the theory that there is no object (*nirviṣayakhyāti*): the acceptance of other theories [such as *asatkhyāti*]—based on the falsity of the object—is refuted by the statement that "the cognition of silver and so forth is indeed without any [objective] delineation."
Nyāyabindu, Chapter 1, Verse 8.
The conclusion.
Therefore, in this case, either a misconception or a cognition of its cause is the error that serves as the basis for a conventional practice that is inconsistent with reality.

Thus ends the first lesson in the chapter on perception within the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrīmad Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians and the independent master of all systems.
